doc.title: Albert Murray interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, September 24, 1997

title: Blues form, memory and high definition
summary: Asked about blues form and Basie, Murray says form gives meaning and connects past to future; digression about digital and high definition video and not changing things until useless.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: What the blues is, and why every jazz player needs it

blocks.x: Can I jump from what you’re saying to the form of the blues, which seems to be so durable — it’s 8, it’s 12-bar or 16-bar — it seems to be so adaptable to different situations, the way the early folk blues singers used it and the way Count Basie used it. That idea of form, does that fit into what you are saying?

Yeah, of course. It’s security. It gives meaning. It keeps things connected. Suppose you couldn’t remember anything. Wouldn’t that be terrible? You couldn’t remember anything. Well you wouldn’t know what to do if you didn’t have anything to remember you see? So you’re obviously not trying to get rid of everything in your past. Because the past as I say is prologue. The door that we are going out of in the future is already there. It was there yesterday. You’re constantly going on that which is there. This media thing we’re doing, that was invented some years ago. It’s already there. It’s a door — we’re going to wipe out that, we’re not going to have any more television, any more tapes, because we’re going to have something else. And then so they just gave you the digitals and they don’t give you what it adds up to. They say this is what we’re doing now. You see the little digits. How would you like that? That would be an innovation, but would you like it? No you would rather that the guy said, well what do they call that, either? The super imaging that you can get on television now? TH: Digital video?
Well but there’s another term they use for the whole thing. There’s another adjective they used to describe it. You know like what, you’ve got virtual reality or something? TH: High definition?

High definition. I mean if a guy comes up and he gets low definition, and he says that’s the latest thing, this is the newest thing is low definition, I mean would you go for that you see? No it’s high definition. I mean you want more of what you have. You want it better. You understand what I’m saying? That’s what we mean by that business of creativity. It’s not a matter of changing. You don’t want to change the thing until it’s useless. Some people can be very insecure about that. They’ve got to be told that this is © Fillius Jazz Archive -8-

better than what they have. To me that’s very understandable. But you do have to be adventurous. You do have to be able to face change and all, but you shouldn’t be idiotic about it. That is, just because it’s new it’s better. We know better than that in the culture in which we live, because we are simply looking for a new market. So if we can put something that cheaper and worse out, but has an effective advertising campaign to sell it, they’re not going to do it better.
